mainTopic: Measuring a cut windpipe, a חכם eating from and buying an animal he permitted, and praise for being strict with oneself and refusing gifts
overview: This amud finishes רב's rule about how much of a cut windpipe makes an animal a טרפה. One version says most of its thickness, and another says most of its open space. In a story, רב starts checking by thickness. His students remind him that he taught 'open space,' so he sends the animal to רבה בר בר חנה. רבה בר בר חנה permits it and buys meat from it. The גמרא then asks three questions. How could a second חכם permit it? Because רב never actually forbade it. How could he eat from an animal he ruled on, given the פסוק in יחזקאל? Because he relied on a tradition from his teachers, not his own reasoning. Wasn't buying the meat suspicious? No, because meat is sold by weight, which is also how רבה answers his wife, the daughter of רב חסדא. The amud ends by praising one who is strict with his own doubtful animal and one who 'hates gifts.' It brings the examples of רבי אלעזר and רבי זירא, whose explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Two versions of רב's measure for a cut windpipe
steps.stepSummary: רב's rule ends with two versions: 'most of its thickness' or 'most of its open space.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Most of its thickness. And some say: most of its open space.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting רב's rule about how much of the windpipe must be cut. It gives two different versions of what he said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Version one measures 'most' by counting the thickness of the windpipe's wall. Version two measures only the hollow inner space and ignores the wall. These can give different answers on the same cut.

keyTerms.meaning: Thickness, counting the wall of the windpipe
The hollow open space inside the windpipe

phrases.english: Most of its thickness,
phrases.notes: This finishes רב's statement from just before, about how much of the windpipe must be cut.

phrases.english: and some say: most of its open space.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב's ruling, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are two versions of רב: a cut windpipe is judged by most of its thickness, or by most of its inner open space.

steps.title: רב checks a cut windpipe by its thickness
steps.stepSummary: An animal with a cut windpipe is brought to רב, and he starts checking it by thickness.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an animal with a cut windpipe that came before רב. He sat and checked it by most of its thickness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a story that shows the two versions in real life. רב is judging an actual case with the 'thickness' measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Checking by thickness fits the first version from step 1. This sets up the problem in the next step, because רב's students remember him teaching the other version.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal whose windpipe is cut through

phrases.english: There was a certain animal with a cut windpipe
that came before רב;

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב וְקָא בָּדֵיק לַהּ בְּרוֹב עוֹבְיָהּ.
phrases.english: he was sitting and checking it by most of its thickness.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא פְּסוּקַת הַגַּרְגֶּרֶת דַּאֲתַאי לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the 'thickness' version being used in a real case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב began judging the animal by the thickness measure.

steps.title: רב's students remind him of what he taught
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא and רב אסי point out that רב taught them to measure by the open space.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא and רב אסי said to רב: Our teacher, you taught us 'most of its open space'!
steps.whatsHappening: Two students challenge רב. They remind him that what he taught them is different from what he is doing now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students are not inventing a new rule. They are quoting רב's own teaching, which is the second version from step 1. This puts pressure on the thickness check.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב:
phrases.english: רב כהנא and רב אסי said to רב:
You taught us, our teacher, by most of its open space!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's thickness check in step 2.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב himself taught the open-space measure, so checking by thickness goes against his own teaching.

steps.title: רבה בר בר חנה permits the animal and buys its meat
steps.stepSummary: רב sends the case to רבה בר בר חנה, who checks by open space, permits it, and buys meat from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב sent it to רבה בר בר חנה. He checked it by most of its open space, declared it kosher, and bought meat from it for thirteen plain איסתירא coins.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. A different חכם checks the animal by the open-space measure, finds it kosher, and even buys some of its meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the open-space measure the cut was not big enough to make the animal a טרפה, so it is permitted. Two questions now come up. Can a second חכם permit this? And can he eat from it himself? The next steps deal with them.
steps.whatToRemember: In practice, the animal was judged by the open-space measure and permitted.

phrases.aramaic: שַׁדְּרֵיהּ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה,
phrases.english: He sent it before רבה בר בר חנה;
he checked it by most of its open space and declared it kosher,
and he bought from it for thirteen
plain איסתירא coins' worth of meat.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁדְּרֵיהּ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the story after the students' reminder.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The animal was checked by the open-space measure and permitted. The ruling חכם even bought its meat.

steps.title: How could a second חכם permit what the first was forbidding?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: once a חכם forbids something, another חכם may not permit it.
steps.simpleTranslation: How could he do this? Isn't it taught: if a חכם declared something impure, his colleague may not declare it pure; if he forbade it, his colleague may not permit it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבה בר בר חנה. רב looked ready to forbid the animal, so how could another חכם permit it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says a second חכם may not overturn the first one's ruling of טמא or אסור. Since רב was checking in a way that pointed toward forbidding, permitting it seems to break this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: How could he do this?: a challenge to someone's action
A חכם who declared something impure

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic rule about rabbinic rulings: one חכם's אסור binds the others.

phrases.english: And how could he do this?
But isn't it taught: a חכם who declared something impure,
his colleague is not allowed to declare it pure;
if he forbade it, his colleague is not allowed to permit it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions רבה בר בר חנה's permitting in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה permitting the animal
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא forbids one חכם from permitting what another forbade, and רב seemed to be forbidding it.

steps.title: רב never actually forbade it
steps.stepSummary: This case is different, because רב never gave a ruling of אסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is different, because רב did not actually forbid it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רב only began checking and then sent the animal on. He never actually said 'forbidden.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא applies only after a real ruling of אסור. Leaning toward forbidding is not a ruling. So רבה בר בר חנה was free to judge the case himself.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not actually forbid it (the doubled verb stresses a real ruling)

phrases.english: Here it is different,
since רב did not actually forbid it.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רב had forbidden the animal, so permitting it would overturn his ruling.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב never gave a ruling, so the ברייתא does not apply.

steps.title: How could he eat from an animal a חכם ruled on?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבה בר בר חנה could eat from an animal he ruled on, quoting יחזקאל's claim that he never ate בשר פגול.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once a חכם has ruled on it, how could he eat from it? Isn't it written: 'Then I said: Alas, Lord God, my soul is not impure; I have not eaten נבלה or טרפה from my youth until now, and no בשר פגול came into my mouth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a second challenge. Even if the animal is kosher, should the חכם who ruled on it eat from it? This step sets up a question that the גמרא will explain next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is not that the animal is forbidden. It is about the חכם who ruled on it then eating from it. The גמרא brings the פסוק in יחזקאל, where the prophet proudly lists foods he never ate. The next step explains how this פסוק connects to a חכם's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that died without proper שחיטה
An animal with a fatal defect
Literally 'disgusting meat'; its meaning here is explained next

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the animal is forbidden. It was ruled kosher. The question is only whether the חכם who ruled on it should eat from it.

phrases.english: And since a חכם has ruled on it,
how could he eat from it?
But isn't it written: "Then I said: Alas, Lord God,
behold, my soul has not become impure;
and I have not eaten a carcass or a tereifa
from my youth until now;
and no piggul meat came into my mouth."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵיוָן דְּאוֹרִי בַּהּ חָכָם, הֵיכִי אֲכַל מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling the permitting question, the גמרא challenges the buying and eating in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה buying and eating meat from the animal he ruled on
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק in יחזקאל suggests a person of high standing avoids certain meat. The גמרא will explain next how this applies to meat a חכם ruled on.

steps.title: The meaning of יחזקאל's three claims
steps.stepSummary: The דרשה explains each of יחזקאל's claims as extra-high standards, including never eating from an animal a חכם had to permit.
steps.simpleTranslation: "My soul has not become impure" means I never had thoughts during the day that would make me impure at night. "I have not eaten נבלה or טרפה" means I never ate from an animal that was so sick people shouted "slaughter it quickly!" "No פיגול meat came into my mouth" means I never ate from an animal that a חכם had to rule on. In the name of רבי נתן they said: it means I never ate from an animal whose gifts for the כהן were not separated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now quotes a teaching that explains each part of the פסוק from the last step. This explanation is what gives the question against רבה בר בר חנה its force.
steps.deeperAnalysis: None of these things is actually forbidden. They are extra-high standards of a very holy person. One of them is not eating from an animal a חכם permitted, and that seems to be exactly what רבה בר בר חנה did.

keyTerms.meaning: "Slaughter it, slaughter it!": an animal so sick it is about to die
Literally, disgusting or rejected meat. Here it is read as meat that needed a ruling
The gifts from an animal given to a כהן

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think these things are forbidden. They are permitted, but a very holy person stays away from them.

phrases.english: "Behold, my soul has not become impure"
means that I did not have improper thoughts during the day
that would bring me to impurity at night;
"And I have not eaten a נבלה or a טרפה"
means that I never ate the meat of
a "slaughter it, slaughter it!" animal;
phrases.notes: An animal so sick that people shout to slaughter it fast before it dies.

phrases.english: "And no פיגול meat came into my mouth"
means that I never ate from an animal
about which a חכם gave a ruling.
In the name of רבי נתן they said:
It means that I never ate from an animal
whose gifts were not separated.
phrases.notes: The gifts are the parts of the animal given to a כהן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Interprets the פסוק quoted in step 7, showing that 'בשר פגול' refers to an animal a חכם ruled on. This is the basis of step 7's question.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה buying meat from the animal he permitted (step 4).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a holy person avoids eating from an animal a חכם permitted, the חכם who ruled on it should surely avoid it.

steps.title: Relying on a tradition is different from relying on reasoning
steps.stepSummary: Avoiding such meat only applies when the ruling came from one's own reasoning. רבה בר בר חנה relied on a tradition he had learned.
steps.simpleTranslation: This only applies to a matter that depends on reasoning. רבה בר בר חנה relied on what he had learned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from יחזקאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra-high standard from the פסוק in יחזקאל is limited to a ruling that rests on a חכם's own reasoning. רבה בר בר חנה ruled based on a tradition he had learned from his teachers, so eating from the animal was not a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: a tradition learned from one's teachers
"These words apply": this rule is limited to

phrases.english: These words apply only
to a matter that depends on reasoning;

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אַגְּמָרֵיהּ סְמַךְ.
phrases.english: רבה בר בר חנה relied on his learning.
phrases.notes: He means a tradition he received from his teachers, not his own reasoning.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the extra-high standard
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any animal a חכם permitted should be avoided.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only rulings based on reasoning. A ruling based on a received tradition is fine to eat from.

steps.title: A new challenge: avoiding suspicion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even so, he should not have bought the meat because people might suspect him, as the ברייתא says to keep away from things that look bad.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you should get the same result because of suspicion, as a ברייתא teaches: if someone judged a case, found someone innocent or guilty, declared something impure or pure, forbade or permitted it, and also witnesses who testified, all of them may buy the item. But the חכמים said: keep away from what looks bad and from anything like it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new reason why רבה בר בר חנה should not have bought the meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answer only showed that the ruling was reliable. This is a different worry: people might think the judge got a good deal as a reward for his ruling. The ברייתא says it is technically allowed, but one should keep away from things that look bad.

keyTerms.meaning: Keep away from what looks bad

steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is a well-known source for a judge or rabbi avoiding even the appearance of a conflict of interest.

phrases.english: But derive it because of suspicion,
phrases.notes: He means: he should not have bought the meat anyway, because people might suspect him.

phrases.english: as it is taught in a ברייתא:
One who judged a case,
found innocent or found guilty,
declared impure or declared pure,
forbade or permitted,
and likewise witnesses who testified:
all of them are allowed to buy the item;
but the חכמים said:

phrases.aramaic: הַרְחֵק מִן הַכִּיעוּר וּמִן הַדּוֹמֶה לוֹ.
phrases.english: Keep away from what looks bad and from what resembles it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the answer of step 9 but raises a different problem.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה buying meat from the animal he permitted (step 4).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even if his ruling was reliable, buying from it looks like he could be getting a reward for his ruling.

steps.title: Meat sold by weight cannot raise suspicion
steps.stepSummary: The worry about suspicion is only for items sold by estimate. Meat is sold by weight, so everyone can see he paid the normal price.
steps.simpleTranslation: This only applies to something sold by estimate. Here, the weight proves it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the suspicion question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a price is just estimated, people might think the judge got a discount. Meat is weighed and sold at the standard price, so it is clear he paid like everyone else.

phrases.english: These words apply only
to an item that is sold by estimate;
here, the weight proves it.
phrases.notes: The scale shows he paid the normal price, so there is no discount to suspect.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to items sold by estimate
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A judge should never buy what he ruled on.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only when the price is estimated. Weighed meat at the standard price raises no suspicion.

steps.title: רבה permitted a טרפה question and bought its meat
steps.stepSummary: A story supports the answer: רבה permitted a possible טרפה and bought meat from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like the story of רבה, who permitted a possible טרפה and bought meat from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story that matches its answer: another חכם also bought meat from an animal he permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה acted exactly like רבה בר בר חנה. This shows that buying weighed meat from an animal you permitted was an accepted practice.

keyTerms.meaning: A possible טרפה, an animal with a question about whether it is fatally injured

phrases.english: This is like the story of רבה,
who permitted a possible טרפה
and bought meat from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life example matching step 11's answer.
steps.raayaObject: That a חכם may buy weighed meat from an animal he permitted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבה buying meat from a טרפה question he permitted.

steps.title: רב חסדא's daughter points to her father's practice
steps.stepSummary: רבה's wife, the daughter of רב חסדא, tells him that her father permitted a בכור but did not buy meat from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The daughter of רב חסדא said to him: Father permitted a בכור but did not buy meat from it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה's wife challenges his behavior by pointing out that her father acted more strictly. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא ruled that a בכור had a blemish that made it permitted, yet he did not buy its meat. This seems to go against רבה buying from the animal he permitted, so the גמרא now needs to explain the difference.

keyTerms.meaning: A firstborn animal (בכור), which may be eaten only after a חכם rules it has a blemish

phrases.english: The daughter of רב חסדא said to him:
Father permitted a בכור
phrases.notes: He ruled it had a blemish, so it could be eaten.

phrases.english: but did not buy meat from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the story of step 12 from another חכם's practice.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה buying meat from the טרפה he permitted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Her father, a great חכם, avoided buying from an animal he permitted, so רבה should have too.

steps.title: רבה explains why a firstborn is different from regular meat
steps.stepSummary: רבה tells his wife that the concern only applies to a בכור, which is sold by estimate. Regular meat is sold by weight, so nobody can suspect him of getting a favor.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: That rule only applies to a בכור, which is sold by estimate. Here, the scale shows the price. What could people suspect? That I got a nicer piece? They sell me a nice piece every day anyway.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers his wife's challenge from her father רב חסדא. He explains why her father's case of a בכור is not like his own case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat from a בכור is sold by guessing its value, so a rabbi who permitted it could quietly get a cheap deal. Ordinary meat is sold by weight, so the price is out in the open. The only possible 'favor' would be a better cut, and רבה gets better cuts every day anyway, so there is nothing to suspect.

keyTerms.meaning: By estimate, by guessing the value
A choice, high-quality piece of meat

steps.whatToRemember: The worry that people will suspect a rabbi of favoritism applies only when the price is not clear, as with a בכור sold by estimate. When meat is sold by weight, the price is plain to everyone.

phrases.english: He said to her: These words apply
phrases.notes: רבה is answering his wife, the daughter of רב חסדא.

phrases.english: to a firstborn, which is sold by estimate;
here, the scale proves it.
phrases.notes: He means the weight shows that I paid the normal price.

phrases.english: What is there to suspect? That I got a choice piece of meat?

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל יוֹמָא אוּמְצָא מְעַלַּיְיתָא זַבִּנוּ לִי.
phrases.english: Every day they sell me a choice piece of meat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לַהּ: הָנֵי מִילֵּי בּוּכְרָא דְּאַשּׁוּמָא מִזְדְּבַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wife's challenge from her father's practice in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: sold by estimate versus sold by weight
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since רב חסדא did not buy meat from a בכור he permitted, רבה should not buy meat from a טרפה case he permitted.
steps.terutzMaskana: A בכור is sold by estimate, so suspicion is possible. Meat sold by weight leaves no room for suspicion, and a choice cut is nothing unusual for רבה.

steps.title: רב חסדא praises one who is strict with his own questionable animal
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says a true תלמיד חכם, and the one described as 'he that hates gifts shall live', is the person who 'sees his own טרפה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Who is a תלמיד חכם? One who sees his own טרפה. And רב חסדא said: Who is meant by 'He that hates gifts shall live'? One who sees his own טרפה.
steps.whatsHappening: The story about permitting and buying meat leads the גמרא into sayings of רב חסדא in praise of a person who is careful with his own questionable animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To 'see his own טרפה' means that when his own animal has a doubtful status, he rules it forbidden and accepts the money loss. רב חסדא calls this the mark of a real תלמיד חכם. He also reads the verse in משלי about hating gifts as describing this person, who does not want to benefit from anything that might not truly be his to enjoy.

keyTerms.meaning: One who rules on his own doubtful טרפה, being strict even at his own loss

steps.confusionAlert: 'Sees his own טרפה' does not mean he simply looks at it. It means that when the doubt involves his own animal, he is strict and forbids it, even though that costs him money.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: אֵיזֶהוּ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם?
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: Who is a Torah scholar?
This is one who sees his own tereifa.
phrases.notes: He means he forbids his own doubtful animal and takes the loss himself.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: אֵיזֶהוּ ״שׂוֹנֵא מַתָּנֹת יִחְיֶה״?
phrases.english: And Rav Chisda said: Who is 'He that hates gifts shall live'?
This is one who sees his own tereifa.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: אֵיזֶהוּ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the specific story to general praise of being strict in one's own doubtful cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A true תלמיד חכם, and the 'hater of gifts' in the verse, is someone who is strict about his own doubtful טרפה.

steps.title: The verse about eating the labor of your hands
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא teaches in the name of רב חסדא that someone who learns, is strict with his own טרפה, and serves scholars is the one described in the verse 'When you eat the labor of your hands, happy shall you be, and it shall be well with you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא taught in the name of רב חסדא: Anyone who reads and learns, sees his own טרפה, and serves Torah scholars, about him the verse says: 'When you eat the labor of your hands, happy shall you be, and it shall be well with you.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another teaching in the name of רב חסדא adds more praise for the person who is strict with his own טרפה. It connects him to a verse in תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three qualities are listed together: learning Torah, being strict with his own doubtful animal, and serving scholars, which is how one learns to rule correctly. Because such a person eats only what is truly his own, the verse about 'the labor of your hands' fits him.

keyTerms.meaning: Served Torah scholars to learn practical ruling from them

phrases.aramaic: דָּרֵשׁ מָר זוּטְרָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב חִסְדָּא:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra expounded in the name of Rav Chisda:
Anyone who reads and learns,
and sees his own tereifa,
and has served Torah scholars –
about him the verse says:
'When you eat the labor of your hands,
happy shall you be, and it shall be well with you.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרֵשׁ מָר זוּטְרָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another teaching of רב חסדא praising the same quality.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who learns, is strict with his own טרפה, and serves scholars fulfills the verse 'When you eat the labor of your hands.'

steps.title: רב זביד: such a person gains both worlds
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד explains that the two parts of the verse promise reward in עולם הזה and in עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: He merits and inherits two worlds, this world and the World to Come. 'Happy shall you be' means in this world, and 'it shall be well with you' means in the World to Come.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד explains the verse that was just quoted and shows what reward it promises.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse has two phrases of blessing, and רב זביד reads each one as a separate reward. 'Happy shall you be' is reward in עולם הזה, and 'it shall be well with you' is reward in עולם הבא.
steps.whatToRemember: Being strict with yourself when the doubt is about your own property is praised strongly. It earns reward in both עולם הזה and עולם הבא.

phrases.aramaic: רַב זְבִיד אָמַר: זוֹכֶה וְנוֹחֵל שְׁנֵי עוֹלָמוֹת,
phrases.english: Rav Zevid said: He merits and inherits two worlds,
this world and the World to Come;
'Happy shall you be' – in this world;
'and it shall be well with you' – in the World to Come.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב זְבִיד אָמַר: זוֹכֶה וְנוֹחֵל שְׁנֵי עוֹלָמוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the verse quoted in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The verse promises reward in both עולם הזה and עולם הבא.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר refuses gifts and invitations from the נשיא
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר would not accept gifts from the house of the נשיא or go when invited, and he quoted the verse 'He that hates gifts shall live.'
steps.simpleTranslation: When they would send רבי אלעזר something from the house of the נשיא, he would not take it, and when they invited him, he would not go. He said: Don't you want me to live? As it is written: 'He that hates gifts shall live.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the verse 'He that hates gifts shall live' and tells how רבי אלעזר lived by it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר took the verse very literally. He refused both gifts and invitations to meals, since he saw both as gifts. He told the נשיא's house that accepting would cost him the long life the verse promises.

keyTerms.meaning: The house of the נשיא, the head of the Jewish community

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר, כִּי הֲווֹ מְשַׁדְּרִי לֵיהּ
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar, when they would send him
something from the house of the Nasi, he would not take it;

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי הֲווֹ מְזַמְּנִי לֵיהּ, לָא אָזֵיל.
phrases.english: and when they would invite him, he would not go.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: לָא קָא בָּעֵי מָר דְּאֵיחֵי?
phrases.english: He said: Does the master not want me to live?
As it is written: 'He that hates gifts shall live.'
phrases.notes: משלי 15:27, the same verse רב חסדא used above.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר, כִּי הֲווֹ מְשַׁדְּרִי לֵיהּ מִבֵּי נְשִׂיאָה מִידֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the verse 'He that hates gifts shall live' from step 15 and shows a sage practicing it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר refused both gifts and invitations, based on 'He that hates gifts shall live.'

steps.title: רבי זירא refuses gifts but accepts invitations
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא also refused gifts, but he did go when invited. The גמרא begins to give his reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they would send רבי זירא something, he would not take it, but when they invited him, he would go. He said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows a second sage who handled this differently. The last word, 'He said', sets up רבי זירא's explanation, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רבי אלעזר, רבי זירא refused gifts. Unlike him, he accepted invitations, so he did not treat an invitation the same as a gift. His reason for the difference starts right after this.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי זֵירָא, כִּי מְשַׁדְּרִי לֵיהּ, לָא שָׁקֵיל,
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira, when they would send him something, he would not take it;
when they would invite him, he would go.
He said:

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זֵירָא, כִּי מְשַׁדְּרִי לֵיהּ, לָא שָׁקֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts רבי זירא's practice with רבי אלעזר's practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי זירא refused gifts but accepted invitations. His reason follows.
